General Principles of Pharmacology - Pharmacodynamics

Slide Companion · current lecture controls scope · graph interpretation emphasized
Drug targetsKd / affinityTwo-state modelPotency vs efficacyAllosteric ligandsPharmacodynamic variabilityTherapeutic index

What this lecture wants you to be able to do

1. Recognize the major categories of molecular targets used by small-molecule drugs and distinguish small molecules from biologic therapies.
2. Use receptor occupancy and the two-state receptor model to distinguish full agonists, partial agonists, neutral competitive antagonists, and inverse agonists.
3. Interpret dose-response and binding curves using affinity (KD), potency, and efficacy.
4. Distinguish orthosteric from allosteric ligands and understand positive versus negative allosteric modulation.
5. Explain sources of pharmacodynamic variability, including desensitization/downregulation and genetic polymorphisms, and calculate/interpret the therapeutic index.
Scope anchor
The final lecture highlight slide names the core buckets directly: important drug targets; small molecules and biologics; two-state model, potency, efficacy; allosteric ligands; genetic polymorphisms; therapeutic index. Use those as the review spine.
01Drug targets: know the categories, not random drug listsTargets
Therapeutic agents are presented in two broad classes: small molecules and biologics. Small molecules remain common, while biologics are increasingly prominent.
Small-molecule target classWhat to recognize
G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs)Very common 7-transmembrane receptor targets with endogenous ligands.
Other receptorsIncludes receptor tyrosine kinases and related signaling receptors.
EnzymesKinases and many other catalytic proteins can be inhibited or modulated.
Ion channelsLigand-gated and voltage-gated channels are druggable.
Nuclear receptors / transcription factorsTargets that can alter gene expression.
Transport / structural proteinsTransporters and structural machinery can be pharmacologic targets.
RNAThe lecture explicitly includes RNA among possible targets.

Biologics

Examples in the lecture include monoclonal antibodies, growth factors, hormones, allergens, and blood factors.

Name clues

The lecture points out useful generic-name stems such as -mab for monoclonal antibodies, -tinib for receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors, -tide for peptides, and -imod for immunomodulators.

02Binding is reversible: KD is an affinity conceptBinding
D + R ⇌ DR     and     KD = k-1/k
High-yield relationship
KD = the drug concentration at which 50% of available receptors are bound. Lower KD means higher affinity; higher KD means lower affinity.
Current-deck occupancy curve: at K_D = 1, half of the available binding sites are occupied. The raw concentration plot is hyperbolic; log concentration makes the relationship appear sigmoidal.
Do not collapse these terms
Affinity is about binding and is represented here by KD. Potency and efficacy describe functional response and are not interchangeable with affinity.
03Two-state receptor model: R versus R*Ligand behavior
For receptors such as GPCRs and ion channels, the lecture uses a two-state model in which receptors equilibrate between an inactive state (R) and an active state (R*). Ligands differ by how they shift, or fail to shift, that equilibrium.
LigandEffect on R ⇌ R*Functional implication
Full agonistShifts strongly toward R*Can produce maximal receptor-system response.
Partial agonistShifts toward R*, but less stronglyLower maximal effect than a full agonist even at high occupancy.
Competitive / neutral antagonistBinds the agonist site but does not favor R or R*Blocks agonist occupancy; effect is surmountable by more agonist.
Inverse agonistShifts toward inactive RReduces constitutive activity; easiest to see when basal activity is substantial.
Full versus partial agonist: both activate the receptor, but the partial agonist plateaus at a lower maximal effect.
Competitive antagonist: the agonist response curve shifts right while the maximum can still be reached with enough agonist.
04Potency is horizontal; efficacy is verticalCurve reading
Fast graph rule
Left-right position = potency. Maximum height = efficacy.
Current-deck conceptual graph: full agonist, partial agonist, neutral antagonist, and inverse agonist are separated by maximal signaling effect and direction relative to basal activity.

Potency

The lecture defines potency as the drug concentration needed to bind/engage the target and illustrates it with left-right shifts. A more potent drug requires a lower concentration for the same response.

Efficacy

Efficacy is the maximal physiological effect the drug can produce. A partial agonist has lower efficacy than a full agonist in the same receptor system.

Fentanyl versus morphine in the lecture: the fentanyl response curve is left-shifted relative to morphine, illustrating greater agonist potency.
Competitive antagonism pattern
A competitive antagonist increases the agonist concentration required for a given effect, producing a rightward shift. Because enough agonist can outcompete it, the maximal response can still be achieved.
05Orthosteric versus allosteric: location mattersAllosterism
Orthosteric site: the site occupied by the natural ligand. Allosteric ligands: bind a different site. The lecture emphasizes that allosteric sites are often less conserved across receptor subtypes, creating an opportunity for subtype selectivity.
Current-deck receptor diagram: the orthosteric binding site and a spatially distinct allosteric binding site occupy different regions of the receptor.
Allosteric modulation can move signaling in either direction: positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) enhance activity; negative allosteric modulators (NAMs) reduce it.
Common trap
Allosteric does not automatically mean inhibitory. Allosteric ligands can be positive or negative modulators.
06Why the same drug can behave differently in different peoplePD variability

Desensitization / downregulation

Repeated or sustained receptor stimulation can reduce responsiveness by altering receptor signaling or receptor abundance.

Pharmacodynamic polymorphisms

Genetic variants in the drug target or downstream signaling machinery can change response even when drug exposure is similar.

The lecture flags receptor desensitization/downregulation and single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) as sources of pharmacodynamic variability.
Clinical pharmacogenomic example in the lecture: cetuximab benefit differs by K-ras status, illustrating how downstream pathway genotype can determine whether blocking the upstream target changes outcome.
Reasoning pattern
If a downstream signaling node is constitutively active, blocking an upstream receptor may fail because the pathway no longer depends on the blocked step.
07Therapeutic index = margin between benefit and toxicitySafety
Therapeutic Index (TI) = TD50 / ED50
Current-deck therapeutic-index diagram: ED50 marks the dose producing the desired effect in 50% of the population; TD50 marks toxicity in 50%. The ratio TD50/ED50 is the therapeutic index.

Larger TI

Greater separation between typical effective and toxic doses; a wider margin of safety.

Smaller TI

Narrower separation between benefit and toxicity; dosing and monitoring must be more precise.

Calculation check
Because TD50 is in the numerator, moving the toxic dose farther away from the effective dose makes the therapeutic index larger, not smaller.
08Exam-ready recall mapIntegrate

If you see KD...

Think affinity / receptor occupancy. Low KD = high affinity.

If one curve is left of another...

Think greater potency, assuming the same response axis.

If one curve plateaus lower...

Think lower efficacy or partial agonism, depending on the setup.

If an antagonist shifts a curve right...

Think competitive / surmountable antagonism when Emax is preserved.

If baseline activity falls below zero/basal...

Think inverse agonist, not neutral antagonist.

If a receptor-site diagram has two pockets...

Natural ligand site = orthosteric; separate regulatory site = allosteric.

If response differs by genotype...

Ask whether the variant is in the target or downstream signaling machinery: that is pharmacodynamic variability.

If safety margin is asked...

Use TI = TD50/ED50.

Before you close this lecture, say these aloud:
  1. Major small-molecule target classes.
  2. Low KD means high affinity.
  3. Full agonist vs partial agonist vs neutral antagonist vs inverse agonist.
  4. Potency = left/right; efficacy = maximal height.
  5. Competitive antagonist shifts right without eliminating Emax.
  6. Orthosteric vs allosteric; PAM vs NAM.
  7. Desensitization/downregulation and pharmacodynamic polymorphisms.
  8. TI = TD50/ED50.
